segments.title: Why the Little Boat Wars were more than motor-boat tactics
segments.summary: An introduction to the Mediterranean war fought by the SBS, commandos, submarines, and small raiding craft rather than a technical survey of motor torpedo boats.
segments.body: The subject is the Mediterranean campaign of maritime special operations rather than a design history of motor torpedo boats and motor launches. It connects the Special Boat Service, Special Boat Section, commandos, and SAS during the Second World War. Small teams reached hostile coasts by folding boat, submarine, requisitioned local craft, and larger raiding boats for reconnaissance or attacks. Together, these methods make the "Little Boat Wars" a story of how British maritime special forces were organised and used.

evidence.note: The opening defines the episode's scope as SBS, SAS, commando, and small-craft operations in the Second World War Mediterranean.

segments.title: Independent Companies and the Royal Marines' expeditionary role
segments.summary: The improvised Independent Companies drew on a ship-borne Royal Marines role, but wartime demands left the Corps without enough manpower to provide them.
segments.body: The Independent Companies grew out of Britain's search for irregular raiding options during the Norway crisis. Their detachments were expected to watch possible landing places and requisition local boats instead of fighting as conventional infantry. These tasks resembled work the Royal Marines already performed from ships. Wartime commitments left the Corps without enough personnel to provide every detachment, so the Army supplied much of the manpower, and some companies later entered the developing commando system.

evidence.note: The lecture connects the Independent Companies to Norway, ship-based Royal Marines work, and the shortage of Royal Marines manpower.

segments.title: Why changing special-forces names complicate the story
segments.summary: The same raiders passed through overlapping organisations and labels, making unit names less reliable than the people and operations they describe.
segments.body: Administrative labels are one of the hardest parts of this history. The people and raids can often be identified more confidently than the unit name applied at a given date. The Special Boat Section, Folding Boat Section, SAS, and other organisations formed, merged, changed names, or disappeared while the war was still under way. Following the people and operations avoids treating every reference to "SBS" as one continuous organisation.

evidence.note: Clarke explains that the raiders are identifiable but their shifting Special Boat, folding-boat, and SAS organisational labels are difficult to untangle.

segments.title: Roger Courtney and the Folding Boat Troop
segments.summary: Roger Courtney's experience with a folding kayak helped turn a personal skill into the small clandestine unit that became the SBS's ancestor.
segments.body: Roger Courtney was an unassuming but unusually capable officer whose pre-war canoeing made a folding kayak a practical military tool. He and his wife had taken Buttercup down the Danube before he brought the boat into wartime service with her blessing. Courtney formed a twelve-man Folding Boat Troop around the ability to travel quietly from a ship or submarine to shore. The unit converted experience with a civilian craft into a specialised maritime-raiding capability.

evidence.note: Clarke describes Courtney's canoe experience, Buttercup, and the formation of the twelve-man Folding Boat Troop.

segments.title: The Glengall infiltration demonstration
segments.summary: When arguments for his unit failed, Courtney used a folding boat to demonstrate how a raider could reach and mark a ship in harbour.
segments.body: Courtney first boarded the landing ship Glengall and returned with a gun cover and other evidence that showed how little notice a small craft could attract. Senior officers then challenged him to repeat the feat against a crew that knew he was coming. He reached the hull, chalked positions where limpet mines might have been placed, and even climbed an inviting rope before entering the captain's trap. Although he was caught, the demonstration proved the concept and secured twelve men and seven additional folding boats.

evidence.note: The account covers Courtney's two approaches to Glengall, the evidence he brought to the meeting, and the resulting expansion of his unit.

segments.title: Submarine-borne reconnaissance at Rhodes
segments.summary: The SBS used HMS Triumph and folding boats to collect the detailed beach intelligence that an ambitious Rhodes raid would have required.
segments.body: Sent to Egypt under Layforce, the SBS was meant to reconnoitre before commando attacks. Rhodes appeared lightly held, and British planners considered either a major raid or an attempt to seize the island, airfield, and harbour with naval gunfire behind the landing force. HMS Triumph carried Courtney, Nigel Willmott, and their folding boat close enough to survey beaches and navigation references over several nights. The final recovery nearly failed when Courtney suffered cramp, lost his signal torch, and was found by Willmott only minutes before an enemy patrol arrived. This was the first major beach reconnaissance of its kind. Both men were decorated, but the intended Rhodes operation came to nothing.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the proposed Rhodes operation, the role of HMS Triumph, and the dangerous multi-night reconnaissance.

segments.title: Mount Etna railway sabotage from a submarine
segments.summary: A tiny SBS party used Malta-based HMS Urge to sabotage a Sicilian railway, extending the submarine's striking power ashore before it returned to conventional combat.
segments.body: The SBS moved from reconnaissance into land sabotage by using submarines of Malta's Tenth Submarine Flotilla as covert transports. After reconnaissance through HMS Urge's periscope, Tug Wilson and a Royal Marine named Hughes landed near a railway tunnel beneath Mount Etna and slipped past fishermen on the beach. They scraped away earth by hand rather than risk the noise of a pickaxe, then fitted a contact mine to the rail. A train approached while they were still finishing the work, forcing them to withdraw without knowing whether the charge had functioned. Urge later raised its periscope in daylight and saw the damaged train and repair crews. The shore team had struck infrastructure beyond the reach of the submarine's own weapons. Urge then sank a cruiser on its withdrawal and survived depth charging, adding the raid to a conventional combat patrol.

evidence.note: Clarke explains the Tenth Submarine Flotilla's raiding role, recounts the rail-mine attack near Mount Etna, and follows HMS Urge through confirmation of the damage, a cruiser sinking, and depth charging.

segments.title: Small raids as a force multiplier
segments.summary: Minor acts of sabotage could impose disproportionate uncertainty, making British raiders look like a wider internal security problem.
segments.body: These carefully chosen, low-level disruptions gave Malta-based submarines another way to hurt the enemy. A two-man landing party could sabotage infrastructure that the submarine could see but could not safely attack with its own weapons. Scattered incidents were difficult to attribute and forced defenders to consider threats along an extensive coastline. Italian authorities could therefore mistake British landings for evidence of a partisan or communist problem. The small raids multiplied uncertainty as well as physical damage.

evidence.note: The lecture explains why apparently modest sabotage amplified the pressure exerted by Malta-based submarines.

segments.title: Courtney's standard for a quiet raider
segments.summary: Courtney sought men who could recognise an overlooked route, act quietly, and leave before the enemy understood what had happened.
segments.body: Courtney wanted raiders who would notice an unlocked side window instead of bursting through the front door firing. His standard favoured stealth, judgement, and imagination over visible aggression. Such men had to find the overlooked route into a target and act without drawing attention. The ideal operation ended before the enemy understood what had happened.

evidence.note: Courtney's recruiting preference is described as finding men who identify and exploit an unobtrusive route into a target.

segments.title: Crete and the misuse of light forces
segments.summary: The battle of Crete shows why a lightly equipped raiding formation could not simply be used as a conventional front-line force.
segments.body: Layforce was committed to regular fighting at Crete even though it had been organised as a fast, lightly equipped raiding force. Later commando formations could fight in the line when they had heavier weapons, fire support, and air power behind them. Crete offered no such coherent support. Senior-command failures and confusion afflicted both sides, while German and Italian forces retained the advantage in the air. The Royal Navy's position worsened when HMS Formidable, its only available carrier and already down to few aircraft, was damaged during an attempt to strike the principal Stuka base.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts Layforce's intended role with its employment at Crete and discusses the lack of supporting combat power.

segments.title: Operation Album and the SBS-SAS divide
segments.summary: Courtney's recall during a change at Combined Operations preceded joint airfield attacks that exposed both the value and the different methods of the SBS and SAS.
segments.body: Roger Keyes's departure from Combined Operations and Louis Mountbatten's tenure there form the background to Courtney's recall to Britain. In the Mediterranean, Operation Album paired the SBS with the SAS in attacks on four airfields and produced a substantial operational effect. It also cost the SBS many men and began a period of serious attrition. The organisations had trained for different methods: SAS mobility suited desert airfield attacks, while folding-boat teams depended on discreet coastal insertion and recovery. David Stirling's successful, expanding SAS organisation drew smaller special units into its orbit because it offered an established structure for special operations. Courtney's maritime raiders lost institutional independence even though their capabilities remained useful.

evidence.note: The transcript links Courtney's recall to the change from Keyes to Mountbatten at Combined Operations, then describes Operation Album, its losses, and the different operational styles of the SBS and SAS.

segments.title: 62 Commando and the small-scale raiding force
segments.summary: 62 Commando used fast boats for larger raids such as Postmaster and Basalt before its surviving elements helped form Jellicoe's later maritime force.
segments.body: Where folding-boat teams emphasised a covert approach, 62 Commando's Small Scale Raiding Force used high-speed boats for larger attacks. Operations Postmaster, Barricade, Riot, Acquaint, and Basalt show the breadth of its work. Basalt was later linked to the background of Hitler's Commando Order after German prisoners were found shot with their hands tied. In this account, they had tried to escape, exposing the grim prisoner-control problem faced by a small raiding party. Every guard assigned to prisoners reduced the strength available for the raid, while limited boat capacity prevented the force from bringing many more men. The force also worked with SOE before disbandment, and its remaining elements joined other special-operations units under George Jellicoe. The wartime SBS consequently inherited both clandestine folding-boat practice and a heavier boat-raiding tradition.

evidence.note: The segment identifies 62 Commando's boat-raiding role, named operations, prisoner-control constraints, work with SOE, disbandment, and the movement of surviving elements toward Jellicoe's command.

segments.title: Why paper strength overstates a raiding unit's power
segments.summary: A nominal establishment says little about how many raiders, berths, and boats are actually available after training injuries and operations.
segments.body: A commando's theoretical establishment of roughly 450 men did not equal its usable strength. High-tempo training caused injuries, while combat added casualties, deaths, and the ordinary physical and mental wear of war. Men also needed rest or time away if the unit was to remain effective. Even after personnel availability was calculated, the number of boats and berths aboard the parent ship imposed a separate hard limit on the force that could actually deploy.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts nominal unit strength with losses, rest requirements, and the transport capacity available for an operation.

segments.title: Jellicoe and the re-formed SBS
segments.summary: After losses and reorganisation, the folding-boat section and 62 Commando became part of an SBS commanded by George Jellicoe.
segments.body: The original folding-boat force had been heavily depleted and drawn into the SAS system as Stirling's successful organisation absorbed smaller special units. Following David Stirling's capture, the formation was divided between the Special Raiding Squadron and a new SBS. That SBS combined the surviving SAS folding-boat element with 62 Commando. Lieutenant Colonel George Jellicoe then commanded a force capable of both clandestine small-boat work and larger maritime raids.

evidence.note: Clarke traces the attrition of the folding-boat section and describes the later SBS reorganisation under Jellicoe.

segments.title: Operation Angelo and the collapse of the independent folding-boat force
segments.summary: Operation Angelo achieved its immediate purpose but inflicted losses severe enough to end the folding-boat section as an independent formation.
segments.body: Operation Angelo achieved considerable success, but only David Sutherland and Duggan avoided capture and returned to the submarines. The loss of the section's captain and so many trained raiders devastated a unit whose strength had already been falling. Tactical success could not preserve the organisation after the loss of so much specialist manpower. What remained was folded into the SAS Folding Boat Section rather than continuing independently.

evidence.note: Clarke describes Operation Angelo as operationally successful but devastating to the folding-boat formation, with only Sutherland and Duggan returning to the submarines.

segments.title: Operation Tenement and the limits of raiding claims
segments.summary: The raid on Symi shows how Jellicoe's SBS combined motor launches and local craft, while also inviting caution about claims of forces tied down.
segments.body: Operation Tenement, the raid on Symi, was a larger maritime operation using ten motor launches alongside schooners and armed caïques. This mixture of craft let Jellicoe's SBS carry more combat power than a two-man folding-boat team and even defeat an encountered German E-boat. Raids across the Aegean, Adriatic, and nearby coasts forced defenders to cover many possible landing points. The resulting claim that six German divisions were tied down also reflected pressure from local partisans and SOE networks, so the effect cannot be credited to the SBS alone.

evidence.note: The lecture describes Operation Tenement's mixed craft and qualifies broad claims about the number of German forces tied down.

segments.title: Anders Lassen and the attrition behind the raids
segments.summary: Lassen's Victoria Cross is set against the deaths, captures, and personal guilt borne by a small pool of experienced maritime raiders.
segments.body: Major Anders Lassen was the only member of the wartime SAS to receive the Victoria Cross. His award sits within a wider account of attrition among maritime raiders: Appleyard and Lassen died, while David Stirling and Tug Wilson were captured. Deaths and captures could strip small formations of scarce experience even when individual operations succeeded. Hughes was too ill to join Wilson's final operation and believed his absence had cost his friend his life. He carried that guilt until he learned that Wilson was alive.

evidence.note: Clarke identifies Lassen's Victoria Cross, then lists the deaths or captures of Appleyard, Lassen, Stirling, and Tug Wilson and recounts Hughes's reaction to Wilson's disappearance.

segments.title: Recruiting for silence, judgement, and submarine discipline
segments.summary: Courtney's recruiting guidance valued the quiet, responsible operator who could protect a submarine and plan for every contingency.
segments.body: The recruitment standard rejects theatrical toughness in favour of someone quiet, responsible, and willing to let a completed mission be the only reward. Courtney's notice contrasts two men in a £15 folding boat with a £350,000 submarine and 52 trained crewmen, while stressing that the submarine's price captured only part of its value to the war effort. One careless act could expose the submarine and every life aboard. Raiders therefore had to understand naval rank, etiquette, secrecy, and the authority of the submarine's captain rather than behave as independent adventurers. They were also expected to check equipment personally, plan for contingencies, and protect scarce folding boats before leaving the parent submarine.

evidence.note: A contemporary recruitment document sets out the desired personal qualities, submarine discipline, and planning responsibilities.

segments.title: Why reconnaissance raiders and airfield attackers needed different methods
segments.summary: Two men landing from a submarine could scout or sabotage discreetly, but airfield attacks demanded more people, more firepower, and a different extraction plan.
segments.body: The SBS model used a small team to place a charge and return to its folding boat, while the SAS operated in mobile desert columns. Vehicles let the SAS bring more men and enough explosives or firepower to attack an airfield, then escape by several possible routes. A foot party landed from a submarine had little support and had to return to one vulnerable beach and the same folding boats. Airfield attacks became more practical when 62 Commando and the Small Scale Raiding Force supplied larger boats that could deliver sufficient mass and extract it quickly.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts desert mobility with the fixed beach extraction problem faced by a submarine-launched folding-boat team.

segments.title: The postwar SBS niche: small teams rather than commando mass
segments.summary: Postwar SBS identity rested on tasks requiring a very small elite group, leaving larger commando assaults to Royal Marines formations.
segments.body: The postwar SBS distinguished itself from wartime formations that had taken on larger raiding roles. Once a covert team is discovered and forced into a prolonged fight, the enemy can reinforce more easily than the raiders can. The Royal Marines' 3 Commando Brigade already provided the larger formations needed for assaults with greater mass, firepower, and transport. The SBS therefore grounded its identity in Courtney's quiet reconnaissance and sabotage tradition, where a very small elite group was more useful than a commando formation.

evidence.note: The conclusion contrasts the postwar SBS's small-team special-operations niche with the larger Royal Marines commando role.
